title: A Passage to Africa
author: George Alagiah
blurb: War reporting from Somalia that questions the ethics of journalism and confronts uncomfortable truths about watching human suffering.
source: Extract from A Passage to Africa (2001)
heading: A Passage to Africa

paragraphs.html: I saw a thousand hungry, lean, scared and betrayed faces as I criss-crossed Somalia between the end of 1991 and December 1992, but there is one I will never forget.

I was in a little hamlet just outside Gufgaduud, a village in the back of beyond, a place the aid agencies had yet to reach. In my notebook I had jotted down instructions on how to get there. 'Take the Badale Road for a few kilometres till the end of the tarmac, turn right on to a dirt track, stay on it for about forty-five minutes — Gufgaduud. Go another fifteen minutes approx. — like a ghost village.'

In the ghoulish manner of journalists on the hunt for the most striking pictures, my cameraman and I tramped from one hut to another. What might have appalled us when we'd started our trip just a few days before no longer impressed us much. The search for the shocking is like the craving for a drug: you require heavier and more frequent doses the longer you're at it. Pictures that stun the editors one day are written off as the same old stuff the next. This sounds callous, but it is just a fact of life. It's how we collect and compile the images that so move people in the comfort of their sitting rooms back home.

There was Amina Abdirahman, who had gone out that morning in search of wild, edible roots, leaving her two young girls lying on the dirt floor of their hut. They had been sick for days, and were reaching the final, enervating stages of terminal hunger. Habiba was ten years old and her sister, Ayaan, was nine. By the time Amina returned, she had only one daughter. Habiba had died. No rage, no whimpering, just a passing away — that simple, frictionless, motionless deliverance from a state of half-life to death itself. It was, as I said at the time in my dispatch, a vision of 'famine away from the headlines, a famine of quiet suffering and lonely death'.

There was the old woman who lay in her hut, abandoned by relations who were too weak to carry her on their journey to find food. It was the smell that drew me to her doorway: the smell of decaying flesh. Where her shinbone should have been there was a festering wound the size of my hand. She'd been shot in the leg as the retreating army of the deposed dictator took revenge on whoever it found in its way. The shattered leg had fused into the gentle V-shape of a boomerang. It was rotting; she was rotting. You could see it in her sick, yellow eyes and smell it in the putrid air she recycled with every struggling breath she took.
And then there was the face I will never forget.

My reaction to everyone else I met that day was a mixture of pity and revulsion. Yes, revulsion. The degeneration of the human body, sucked of its natural vitality by the twin evils of hunger and disease, is a disgusting thing. We never say so in our TV reports. It's a taboo that has yet to be breached. To be in a feeding centre is to hear and smell the excretion of fluids by people who are beyond controlling their bodily functions. To be in a feeding centre is surreptitiously to wipe your hands on the back of your trousers after you've held the clammy palm of a mother who has just cleaned vomit from her child's mouth.

There's pity, too, because even in this state of utter despair they aspire to a dignity that is almost impossible to achieve. An old woman will cover her shrivelled body with a soiled cloth as your gaze turns towards her. Or the old and dying man who keeps his hoe next to the mat with which, one day soon, they will shroud his corpse, as if he means to go out and till the soil once all this is over.

I saw that face for only a few seconds, a fleeting meeting of eyes before the face turned away, as its owner retreated into the darkness of another hut. In those brief moments there had been a smile, not from me, but from the face. It was not a smile of greeting, it was not a smile of joy — how could it be? — but it was a smile nonetheless. It touched me in a way I could not explain. It moved me in a way that went beyond pity or revulsion.

What was it about that smile? I had to find out. I urged my translator to ask the man why he had smiled. He came back with an answer. 'It's just that he was embarrassed to be found in this condition,' the translator explained. And then it clicked. That's what the smile had been about. It was the feeble smile that goes with apology, the kind of smile you might give if you felt you had done something wrong.

Normally inured to stories of suffering, accustomed to the evidence of deprivation, I was unsettled by this one smile in a way I had never been before. There is an unwritten code between the journalist and his subjects in these situations. The journalist observes, the subject is observed. The journalist is active, the subject is passive. But this smile had turned the tables on that tacit agreement. Without uttering a single word, the man had posed a question that cut to the heart of the relationship between me and him, between us and them, between the rich world and the poor world. If he was embarrassed to be found weakened by hunger and ground down by conflict, how should I feel to be standing there so strong and confident?

I resolved there and then that I would write the story of Gufgaduud with all the power and purpose I could muster. It seemed at the time, and still does, the only adequate answer a reporter can give to the man's question.

I have one regret about that brief encounter in Gufgaduud. Having searched through my notes and studied the dispatch that the BBC broadcast, I see that I never found out what the man's name was. Yet meeting him was a seminal moment in the gradual collection of experiences we call context. Facts and figures are the easy part of journalism. Knowing where they sit in the great scheme of things is much harder. So, my nameless friend, if you are still alive, I owe you one.

a1.quote: I saw a thousand hungry, lean, scared and betrayed faces
a1.what: The list moves from the body ('hungry, lean') to feelings ('scared'), then ends on the unexpected 'betrayed'.
a1.effect: 'Betrayed' suggests someone is to blame: this famine has human causes.

a2.quote: Somalia between the end of 1991 and December 1992,
a2.what: Somalia fell into civil war in 1991 when the dictator Siad Barre was overthrown. The fighting made a famine far worse, killing an estimated 300,000 people. Alagiah, a BBC reporter, wrote this memoir in 2001.

a3.what: From 'a thousand' faces Alagiah singles out 'one', and the 'I' makes this a personal memory.
a3.effect: We are hooked, wanting to know whose face it is.

a4.what: What kind of writing does 'one I will never forget' prepare you for: a news report or something personal? Does the promise of an unforgettable face make you want to read on? Why?

a5.quote: a village in the back of beyond,
a5.what: 'The back of beyond' is a relaxed, almost jokey saying for somewhere very remote.
a5.effect: The casual tone suggests a writer keeping horror at arm's length.

a7.quote: the aid agencies had yet to reach.
a7.what: Groups like UNICEF, the Red Cross and Médecins Sans Frontières (Doctors Without Borders) could not keep up with the crisis. Many rural areas waited weeks or months for help, and journalists sometimes arrived first.

a6.quote: a place the aid agencies had yet to reach. In my notebook I had jotted down instructions on how to get there.
a6.what: Everyday words like 'jotted down' make a trip into a crisis sound routine.
a6.effect: This controlled voice makes the horror hit harder when it breaks through.

a8.quote: Take the Badale Road for a few kilometres till the end of the tarmac, turn right on to a dirt track, stay on it for about forty-five minutes — Gufgaduud. Go another fifteen minutes approx. — like a ghost village.
a8.what: Copying his clipped notebook directions, down to 'approx.', shows this is a real route.
a8.effect: The dull practical detail makes the final 'ghost village' more chilling.

a9.what: Why does Alagiah copy out his actual notebook directions? What do 'approx.' and 'like a ghost village' do to you? Do you feel you are travelling with him?

a10.quote: In the ghoulish manner of journalists on the hunt for the most striking pictures,
a10.what: 'Ghoulish' links journalists to ghouls that feed on the dead, and Alagiah includes himself.
a10.effect: Because he criticises himself first, we trust his honesty.

a11.quote: What might have appalled us when we'd started our trip just a few days before no longer impressed us much.
a11.what: The mild phrase 'no longer impressed us much' is an understatement (making something sound smaller than it is).
a11.effect: It shows how quickly, in 'a few days', people grow numb.

a12.quote: The search for the shocking is like the craving for a drug: you require heavier and more frequent doses the longer you're at it.
a12.what: Alagiah compares hunting for shocking pictures to a drug habit needing 'heavier and more frequent doses'.
a12.effect: Journalism looks like an addiction, and the word 'you' suggests we share the craving.

a13.quote: This sounds callous, but it is just a fact of life.
a13.what: Alagiah admits this 'sounds callous' (cold and uncaring). Is 'just a fact of life' a fair excuse? Who is really to blame for the hunger for shocking images: journalists, or the viewers who watch them?

a14.quote: It's how we collect and compile the images that so move people in the comfort of their sitting rooms back home.
a14.what: Who does 'people in the comfort of their sitting rooms' describe? Where are you reading this right now? Does the phrase make you feel part of the story, or far away from it?

a15.what: Alagiah gives Amina her full name, turning a 'victim' back into a person.
a15.effect: This sets up the ending, where he admits he never learned the smiling man's name.

a16.quote: Habiba was ten years old and her sister, Ayaan, was nine.
a16.what: Why does Alagiah tell us the girls' exact ages? How would it feel different if he had just written 'two young girls'? Which detail stays with you most, and why?

a17.quote: No rage, no whimpering, just a passing away — that simple, frictionless, motionless deliverance from a state of half-life to death itself.
a17.what: 'No rage, no whimpering' lists what did not happen, so the death feels silent and empty.
a17.effect: Calling death 'deliverance' (rescue) suggests it was a release from 'half-life'.

a18.quote: It was, as I said at the time in my dispatch, a vision of
a18.what: Alagiah falls back on the words of his old 'dispatch' and keeps his present feelings out.
a18.effect: The restraint shows how much he is holding back.

a19.quote: 'famine away from the headlines, a famine of quiet suffering and lonely death'.
a19.what: 'Quiet suffering and lonely death' is polished writing, and Alagiah knows he crafted it.
a19.effect: We notice the gap between real pain and the neat words used to report it.

a20.quote: abandoned by relations who were too weak to carry her on their journey to find food.
a20.what: 'Abandoned' sounds cruel, but the relatives were simply 'too weak' to carry her.
a20.effect: Alagiah refuses to judge, showing how famine forces impossible choices.

a21.quote: It was the smell that drew me to her doorway: the smell of decaying flesh.
a21.what: Repeating 'smell' and holding 'decaying flesh' back until after the colon makes the worst detail land last.
a21.effect: Smell is hard to shut out, so we cannot keep this distant.

a22.quote: a festering wound the size of my hand.
a22.what: Alagiah measures the 'festering' (rotting) wound against his own hand.
a22.effect: We can picture its exact size, and his own body is tied to her suffering.

a23.quote: the retreating army of the deposed dictator
a23.what: As Siad Barre's government collapsed, his retreating soldiers attacked civilians. By naming who shot her, Alagiah shows that this suffering had human causes. War and politics, as well as famine, are to blame.

a24.quote: It was rotting; she was rotting.
a24.what: Only one word changes between the two clauses: 'it' (the leg) becomes 'she'.
a24.effect: The woman and her wound merge, as if her whole self is decaying.

a25.quote: You could see it in her sick, yellow eyes and smell it in the putrid air she recycled with every struggling breath she took.
a25.what: Soon Alagiah will admit to 'revulsion'. How do you respond to the 'sick, yellow eyes' and 'putrid air'? Do you feel only sympathy, or something else as well? Why might he describe her so graphically?

a26.quote: And then there was the face I will never forget.
a26.what: This single sentence stands alone after three paragraphs of horror, repeating the opening promise.
a26.effect: The pause signals a turn from many victims to one person.

a27.what: Why does this sentence have a paragraph to itself? How does it change the speed of your reading? After so much horror, does it make you feel curious, relieved or uneasy?

a28.what: The two-word sentence repeats 'revulsion' (disgust), as if answering our shock without softening it.
a28.effect: Journalists rarely admit disgust at their subjects, so the confession feels uncomfortably honest.

a29.quote: The degeneration of the human body, sucked of its natural vitality by the twin evils of hunger and disease, is a disgusting thing.
a29.what: Alagiah calls the dying body 'a disgusting thing'. Does this admission make him seem honest, or does it disturb you? Can you respect someone for saying something this difficult?

a31.quote: our TV reports. It's a taboo that has yet to be breached.
a31.what: In the 1990s, 24-hour TV news changed how wars and famines were reported. Shocking footage could push governments to act (the 'CNN effect'), but it also pressured reporters to find ever more shocking images.

a30.quote: We never say so in our TV reports. It's a taboo that has yet to be breached.
a30.what: Alagiah admits TV news never shows reporters' disgust, a 'taboo' (something no one may say).
a30.effect: By breaking it here, he earns our trust.

a32.quote: To be in a feeding centre is surreptitiously to wipe your hands on the back of your trousers after you've held the clammy palm of a mother who has just cleaned vomit from her child's mouth.
a32.what: 'Your' puts us in the reporter's body, and 'surreptitiously' (secretly) makes the wipe a hidden, shameful act.
a32.effect: We have to ask whether we would do the same.

a33.what: How does it feel to imagine wiping 'your hands' after holding that mother's palm? Does 'you' make you care more, or feel pressured? Why does Alagiah put you in his place?

a34.quote: they aspire to a dignity that is almost impossible to achieve.
a34.what: Alagiah uses a paradox (a seeming contradiction): people in 'utter despair' still 'aspire to' dignity.
a34.effect: We see their pride as well as their pain, which deepens our respect.

a36.quote: An old woman will cover her shrivelled body with a soiled cloth as your gaze turns towards her. Or the old and dying man who keeps his hoe next to the mat with which, one day soon, they will shroud his corpse, as if he means to go out and till the soil once all this is over.
a36.what: The dying man keeps his hoe, a farming tool, beside the mat that will be his shroud.
a36.effect: The hoe symbolises a stubborn hope for a future he will never have.

a35.quote: An old woman will cover her shrivelled body with a soiled cloth as your gaze turns towards her. Or the old and dying man who keeps his hoe next to the mat with which, one day soon, they will shroud his corpse, as if he means to go out and till the soil once all this is over.
a35.what: The woman covers herself 'as your gaze turns towards her': even dying, she minds being stared at.
a35.effect: It introduces the shame of being watched, key to the smile later.

a37.what: The dying man keeps the hoe he would use if he got better. What does this make you feel? Does Alagiah want you to see these people as victims, or as something more?

a38.quote: I saw that face for only a few seconds, a fleeting meeting of eyes before the face turned away, as its owner retreated into the darkness of another hut.
a38.what: Phrases like 'a fleeting meeting of eyes' slow the writing down to one brief moment.
a38.effect: After a flood of horrors, this feels quiet and personal, and we lean in.

a39.quote: It was not a smile of greeting, it was not a smile of joy — how could it be? — but it was a smile nonetheless.
a39.what: Repeating 'it was not a smile of' rules out greeting and joy without finding an answer.
a39.effect: The mystery pulls us on to discover what the smile meant.

a40.quote: It touched me in a way I could not explain. It moved me in a way that went beyond pity or revulsion.
a40.what: Before reading on, what do you think the smile means? Alagiah says he 'could not explain' it. Does a detail without an easy answer frustrate you, or draw you further in?

a41.quote: What was it about that smile? I had to find out.
a41.what: A short question and a short reply show the reporter springing into action.
a41.effect: The quicker pace builds suspense: we want the answer too.

a42.quote: 'It's just that he was embarrassed to be found in this condition,' the translator explained.
a42.what: 'Just' makes the man's embarrassment sound small and natural to him.
a42.effect: The dying man feels ashamed, yet we sense the shame belongs to the well-fed onlookers.

a43.quote: And then it clicked. That's what the smile had been about. It was the feeble smile that goes with apology, the kind of smile you might give if you felt you had done something wrong.
a43.what: The man feels he has 'done something wrong'. Does this surprise you? What does it suggest about how we view people in poverty? How should the journalist, and the reader, feel now?

a44.quote: Normally inured to stories of suffering, accustomed to the evidence of deprivation, I was unsettled by this one smile in a way I had never been before.
a44.what: 'Inured' means hardened, so Alagiah admits his numbness before saying this 'one smile' broke through.
a44.effect: It is the turning point: his professional shield cracks.

a45.quote: The journalist observes, the subject is observed. The journalist is active, the subject is passive.
a45.what: Two balanced sentences use antithesis (opposites side by side): the journalist is 'active', the subject 'passive'.
a45.effect: The rule-like pattern shows a fixed, unequal relationship, which the smile has just broken.

a46.quote: But this smile had turned the tables on that tacit agreement.
a46.what: 'Turned the tables' means the silent smile has reversed who holds the power.
a46.effect: Suddenly the powerful journalist feels judged by the powerless man.

a47.quote: between the rich world and the poor world.
a47.what: The three 'between' phrases (a tricolon) widen from 'me and him' to 'the rich world and the poor world'.
a47.effect: One small moment comes to stand for global inequality, including us.

a49.what: In 1994 Kevin Carter won a Pulitzer Prize for a photo of a starving Sudanese child watched by a vulture. Critics asked why he did not help. Alagiah faces a similar question here.

a48.quote: If he was embarrassed to be found weakened by hunger and ground down by conflict, how should I feel to be standing there so strong and confident?
a48.what: The man never speaks, yet Alagiah says he 'posed a question'. In your own words, what is that question? Does it make you think about your own comfort and safety as you read?

a50.quote: I resolved there and then that I would write the story of Gufgaduud with all the power and purpose I could muster.
a50.what: Alagiah resolves to write, and the alliteration in 'power and purpose' makes the promise sound firm.
a50.effect: He cannot feed the man, but he can make the world see him.

a51.quote: It seemed at the time, and still does, the only adequate answer a reporter can give to the man's question.
a51.what: Alagiah calls writing 'the only adequate answer a reporter can give'. Do you agree? Can writing about suffering ever be enough? How does this fit with the 'ghoulish' hunt for pictures earlier?

a52.quote: Having searched through my notes and studied the dispatch that the BBC broadcast, I see that I never found out what the man's name was.
a52.what: Alagiah named Amina and her daughters, yet never learned the name of the man who changed him most.
a52.effect: Admitting this quiet irony makes us trust him more.

a53.quote: Yet meeting him was a seminal moment in the gradual collection of experiences we call context. Facts and figures are the easy part of journalism. Knowing where they sit in the great scheme of things is much harder.
a53.what: 'Seminal' means hugely important: this meeting shaped how Alagiah understands the 'facts and figures' he reports.
a53.effect: 'We call context' hints the usual word is too small for what he learned.

a54.quote: my nameless friend, if you are still alive, I owe you one.
a54.what: Speaking directly to his 'nameless friend', Alagiah admits with 'if you are still alive' that he may be dead.
a54.effect: The casual 'I owe you one' feels raw and real.

a55.what: Why end such a serious piece with the casual 'I owe you one'? What does 'if you are still alive' add? How does ending on uncertainty leave you feeling?
